title: Number systems fully solvable by analysis show only simple behavior

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Number systems fully solvable by analysis show only simple behavior

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Systems based on numbers that traditional mathematics (e.g. calculus) can analyze completely end up showing only fairly simple behavior; textbook systems are selected for analyzability and therefore are simple.

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: Inevitably, however, when such complete analysis is possible, the final behavior that is found is fairly simple.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 4, “Systems Based on Numbers”; section “The Notion of Numbers” (from p. 115), p. 115. Scope: number-based systems treated in traditional science and mathematics

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch04-01: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.35

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Literature and textbook corpora can test restricted associations and search for counterexamples. They cannot provide unbiased coverage of all number-based systems or cleanly separate analyzability from historical selection.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Define complete analytic solvability and behavioral complexity for a fixed corpus of textbook dynamical systems, then test their association while controlling for pedagogical selection. Counterexamples of completely solved systems with complex behavior would refute the absolute form.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
The scope mixes a mathematical universal with a sociological explanation.

Textbook selection creates strong ascertainment bias.

Complete analysis and fairly simple are ambiguous.

fields.value:

analysis feasibility: 0.35
discriminating power: 0.3
data adequacy: 0.22
data existence: 0.55

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Wolfram's point is that when calculus and similar methods finish the job, the behavior they find is simple, and that textbooks are chosen for that amenability. That connection is built into what those methods can express. A survey of solved textbook systems would reproduce the selection rather than test a further empirical claim about number-based systems.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: The claim ties 'complete analysis by traditional mathematics' to 'fairly simple behavior' and explains textbook examples by that selection. Systems that traditional methods can solve are simple in the sense of those methods, so the outcome does not separate a factual regularity from the definition of analyzability.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
The claim is close to a selection effect: textbooks keep systems that traditional analysis can finish, and those systems are then called simple.

There is no independent catalog of 'all number-based systems traditional mathematics can analyze completely' whose behavior could come out complex.

analysis feasibility: 0.35
